2013|paper-1a|1.question:
Which of the following statements about boiling and evaporation of a liquid is/are correct?

(1) A liquid absorbs energy when it boils but does not absorb energy when it evaporates.

(2) Boiling occurs at a definite temperature while evaporation takes place above room temperature.

(3) Boiling occurs throughout the liquid while evaporation only takes place at the liquid's surface.

A. (1) only

B. (3) only

C. (1) and (2) only

D. (2) and (3) only
2013|paper-1a|1.reasoning:
Both processes require latent heat, so (1) is false. Evaporation can occur below room temperature, so (2) is false; at a fixed external pressure boiling occurs at the boiling point.

Vapour bubbles form throughout a boiling liquid, whereas evaporation is escape from the surface. Only (3) is correct: B.

2013|paper-1a|10.question:
Two identical spheres move in opposite directions with speeds u and v (u > v) and make a head-on collision. Which diagrams show possible situations after collision?

A. (1) only

B. (3) only

C. (1) and (2) only

D. (2) and (3) only
2013|paper-1a|10.reasoning:
Take right as positive. Initial momentum is m(u−v) > 0. In (1), final momentum is −mu, so it cannot be conserved. In (2), the spheres exchange velocities, conserving both momentum and kinetic energy: possible.

In (3), momentum conservation requires mu−mv = mv, or u = 2v, which is allowed by u > v. Kinetic energy decreases from ½m(4v²+v²) to ½mv², so an inelastic collision is possible. Therefore (2) and (3): D. The word possible does not mean for every u and v.

2013|paper-1a|11.question:
Particles P and Q start at the same position and travel along the same straight line. Their velocity-time graph is shown. Which descriptions are correct?

(1) At t = 1 s, P changes its direction of motion.

(2) At t = 2 s, the separation between P and Q is 4 m.

(3) At t = 4 s, P and Q meet.

A. (1) only

B. (2) only

C. (1) and (3) only

D. (2) and (3) only
2013|paper-1a|11.reasoning:
A direction reversal requires velocity to change sign. At 1 s, P still has negative velocity; only its acceleration changes sign. P reverses at 2 s, so (1) is false.

Signed areas give xP(2) = −½(2)(2) = −2 m and xQ(2) = ½(2)(2) = 2 m: separation 4 m, so (2) is true. At 4 s, xP = −2+½(2)(4) = 2 m, while xQ = ½(4)(4) = 8 m. Equal velocities at 4 s do not mean equal positions. Only (2): B.

2013|paper-1a|12.question:
A 50 g bullet fired at 400 m s−1 passes through a fixed wooden block of thickness 6 cm and emerges at 250 m s−1. Find the average resistive force of the block on the bullet. Neglect air resistance and gravity.

A. 4.06×104 N

B. 1.02×104 N

C. 125 N

D. Cannot be found because the travel time inside the block is unknown.
2013|paper-1a|12.reasoning:
Convert m = 0.050 kg and d = 0.060 m. Work against resistance equals the loss of kinetic energy: Favgd = ½m(u²−v²).

Favg = 0.5(0.050)(400²−250²)/0.060 = 40625 N ≈ 4.06×104 N, opposite to motion: A. Time is unnecessary for this work-energy calculation.

2013|paper-1a|13.question: * A particle is projected at t = 0 and follows the parabolic path shown before landing. Which graph represents its kinetic energy (KE) against time before landing? Neglect air resistance.
2013|paper-1a|13.reasoning:
Horizontal velocity ux is constant; vertical velocity is uy−gt. Thus KE(t) = ½m[ux²+(uy−gt)²], a smooth upward-opening parabola.

At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is not, so the minimum KE is positive. The curve is D, not the V-shaped B or the zero-minimum C.

2013|paper-1a|14.question:
A semicircular cardboard hangs at O from a spring balance reading 5 N. Which statements are correct?

(1) Its weight is 5 N.

(2) Its centre of gravity is directly under O.

(3) The reading would become zero on the Moon's surface.

A. (1) and (2) only

B. (1) and (3) only

C. (2) and (3) only

D. (1), (2) and (3)
2013|paper-1a|14.reasoning:
In static equilibrium the upward balance force equals the weight: 5 N. Zero torque about the suspension point requires the weight line to pass vertically through O, with the centre of gravity below O in this stable hanging position.

The Moon has a nonzero gravitational field, so the reading decreases but is not zero. Statements (1) and (2) only: A.

2013|paper-1a|15.question:

2013|paper-1a|16.question:
The snapshot shows a continuous transverse wave travelling along x at t = 0. At t = 1.5 s, particle P passes its equilibrium position for the second time. Find the wave speed.

A. 20 cm s−1

B. 12 cm s−1

C. 6 cm s−1

D. 4 cm s−1

The equivalent downward zero crossings are at x = 6 and 30 cm, giving λ = 24 cm. P begins at a crest and passes equilibrium at T/4 and 3T/4.

Thus 3T/4 = 1.5 s, T = 2.0 s and v = λ/T = 12 cm s−1: B. The second crossing is not at T/2.

2013|paper-1a|17.question:
Figure (1) shows equilibrium positions a to k, separated by 5 cm. A longitudinal wave travels right at 80 cm s−1. Figure (2) shows the particle positions at one instant. Find amplitude and frequency.

A. 6 cm; 2 Hz

B. 6 cm; 4 Hz

D. 9 cm; 4 Hz
2013|paper-1a|17.reasoning:
Compare each labelled particle with its own equilibrium position. The largest displacement is 6 cm (e.g. d or h), not the separation between neighbouring particles.

Consecutive compression centres are b and j, eight equilibrium spacings apart: λ = 8(5) = 40 cm. Therefore f = v/λ = 80/40 = 2 Hz; amplitude 6 cm and frequency 2 Hz: A.

2013|paper-1a|18.question:
A vibrator generates a stationary wave on a string fixed at one end. The figure shows the string at one instant. Which descriptions must be correct?

(1) P and Q are momentarily at rest at this instant.

(2) Q and R take the same time to reach their respective equilibrium positions.

(3) P and R are always in antiphase.

A. (1) only

B. (3) only

C. (1) and (2) only

D. (2) and (3) only
2013|paper-1a|18.reasoning:
A stationary-wave snapshot does not establish that the oscillation is at its maximum displacement. P is at a spatial crest, but that alone does not establish zero instantaneous particle velocity; (1) need not hold.

All non-node particles pass equilibrium simultaneously. Particles in adjacent loops, such as P and R, oscillate in antiphase. Thus (2) and (3) must hold: D. Different amplitudes do not imply different periods.

2013|paper-1a|19.question:
On a planet, astronauts P and Q stand 400 m and 600 m from a vertical cliff respectively, as shown in top view. P claps once and Q hears two sounds 4 s apart. Find the speed of sound in the planet's atmosphere.

A. 100 m s−1

B. 150 m s−1

C. 200 m s−1

D. 250 m s−1
2013|paper-1a|19.reasoning:
The direct sound travels PQ = 600−400 = 200 m. The reflected sound travels P to cliff to Q: 400+600 = 1000 m.

The 4 s delay corresponds to the extra 1000−200 = 800 m, so v = 800/4 = 200 m s−1: C. It is neither the full echo travel time nor the travel time from the cliff alone.

2013|paper-1a|2.question:
In an experiment to measure the specific latent heat of vaporization of water, a beaker of water is boiled off using an electric heater. Which source of error would lead to an experimental result smaller than the standard value?

A. Energy is lost to the surroundings.

B. Water splashes out of the beaker.

C. Steam condenses on the cooler part of the heater and drops back to the beaker.

D. The heater is not completely immersed in water.
2013|paper-1a|2.reasoning:
The calculation is l = Pt/Δm, treating the measured mass loss as evaporated water. Splashing makes Δm too large without requiring vaporization energy, so the calculated l is too small: B.

Heat loss and incomplete immersion waste input energy, tending to overestimate l. Returning condensate reduces measured mass loss, also increasing Pt/Δm.

2013|paper-1a|20.question:
A ray travels from transparent medium X to air at 40° to the boundary plane. The angle between the refracted ray in air and reflected ray in X is 70°. Find the refractive index of X.

A. sin 40° / sin 30°

B. sin 30° / sin 40°

C. sin 60° / sin 50°

D. sin 50° / sin 60°
2013|paper-1a|20.reasoning:
Angles in Snell's law are measured from the normal: i = 90°−40° = 50°. The reflected ray is 40° below the interface, so the refracted ray is 70°−40° = 30° above it, giving r = 60°.

nXsin 50° = 1 sin 60°; hence nX = sin 60°/sin 50°: C. The result is greater than one, as expected for the stated medium-to-air refraction.

2013|paper-1a|21.question:
White light is resolved into component colours by a glass prism. Which statements are correct?

(1) The refractive indices of glass for different component colours are not the same.

(2) Red light travels faster than violet light in a vacuum.

(3) All component frequencies decrease on entering the prism.

A. (1) only

B. (3) only

C. (1) and (2) only

D. (2) and (3) only

Dispersion occurs because glass has different refractive indices for different frequencies, producing different deviations: (1) is true.

All colours travel at c in a vacuum, so (2) is false. Crossing a stationary boundary changes speed and wavelength, not frequency, so (3) is false. Only (1): A.

2013|paper-1a|22.question:
A point source X on the principal axis of a thin convex lens emits a ray that reaches the axis at Y after refraction. O is the optical centre; OX = 20 cm and OY > OX. Which statements are correct?

(1) The focal length is shorter than 20 cm.

A. (1) only

B. (2) only

C. (1) and (3) only

D. (2) and (3) only

A real image forms with u = 20 cm and v > 20 cm. From 1/f = 1/u+1/v, f < u, so (1) is true. Increasing u increases 1/v and decreases v, so (2) is false.

By reversibility, a source at Y images at X. The magnification is OX/OY < 1, hence diminished. Statements (1) and (3): C.

2013|paper-1a|23.question:
* Monochromatic light forms bright fringes after passing through a diffraction grating. Which arrangement gives the greatest angle θ between the central and first-order bright fringes? Options give grating lines per mm and colour.

A. 400; green

2013|paper-1a|24.question:
Two small identical metal spheres X and Y carry −2Q and +6Q. At their separation the electrostatic force magnitude is F.

They touch and are returned to their original positions. The force becomes

A. F/4, attractive

B. F/4, repulsive

C. F/3, attractive

Total charge is −2Q+6Q = 4Q. Identical spheres share it equally, leaving +2Q on each, so the new force is repulsive.

At the same separation, F′/F = |(2Q)(2Q)|/|(−2Q)(6Q)| = 4/12 = 1/3. Thus F/3, repulsive: D.

2013|paper-1a|25.question:

Uniform-field potential difference V = Ed = (3×106)(500) = 1.5×109 V.

Energy scale QV = 20(1.5×109) = 3×1010 J, giving the listed order 1010 J: C. This is an order estimate, not a detailed time-dependent discharge model.

2013|paper-1a|26.question:
A straight wire carrying current into the paper lies between magnetic pole pieces X and Y. The resultant field is shown. Find the polarity of X and direction of magnetic force on the wire. Ignore Earth's field.

A. N; right

B. N; left

For current into the paper and external field upward, Fleming's left-hand rule (Iℓ × B) gives force to the right: C. Use the external field for the wire force, not its own circular field.

2013|paper-1a|27.question:
Four insulated long straight wires P, Q, R and S in one plane carry equal currents as shown. O is in the plane and equidistant from each wire. Removing which wire increases the magnetic field strength at O?

A. P

2013|paper-1a|28.question: A copper rod XY lies on smooth conducting rails inclined at θ to the horizontal. A magnetic field acts vertically down and a battery is connected as shown. Which diagram gives the magnetic force FB viewed from end Y?

The battery's positive (long-line) terminal is connected to the Y rail, so conventional current passes from Y to X. Viewed from Y towards X, current goes into the view.

With B vertically down, Iℓ × B is horizontal to the left: C. The magnetic force must be perpendicular to B; it is not along the sloping rails. Components of force, rather than the entire magnetic force, act along the rails.

2013|paper-1a|29.question:
A metal rod OP rotates clockwise about O in the paper plane in a uniform magnetic field into the paper. Which statement is correct?

2013|paper-1a|3.question:
* In which situations would the r.m.s. speed of the molecules of a fixed mass of an ideal gas increase?

(1) The gas is heated under constant volume.

(2) The gas expands under constant pressure.

A. (1) only

B. (3) only

C. (1) and (2) only

(1) Heating at constant volume raises T. (2) At constant pressure and fixed mass, V/T is constant, so expansion raises T. (3) Isothermal compression leaves T and r.m.s. speed unchanged. Choose C.

2013|paper-1a|30.question:
Identical resistors X, Y and Z are connected as shown. A battery of negligible internal resistance supplies total power 24 W. Find the power dissipated in Z.

A. 3 W

B. 4 W

C. 6 W

D. 8 W

X is in series with the parallel pair Y and Z. If each branch current is i, X carries 2i. Since P = I²R, PX : PY : PZ = 4 : 1 : 1.

Z therefore dissipates one sixth of the total: 24/6 = 4 W, B. Equal resistances do not imply equal powers when their currents differ.

2013|paper-1a|31.question:
In both circuits the cells have constant e.m.f. and negligible internal resistance. As each rheostat slider S moves right from its mid-position, how do the brightnesses of L1 and L2 change?

In the left circuit the section to the right of the slider is bypassed. Moving S right lengthens the effective series resistance, reducing current and making L1 dimmer.

L2 is directly across an ideal cell; changing the parallel rheostat changes total current but not the bulb voltage. L2 remains unchanged: A.

2013|paper-1a|32.question:
The cell has negligible internal resistance. Closing S leaves both bulbs unlit; the voltmeter has a reading but the ammeter reads zero. If there is only one fault, which is possible?

If Y were open, the source would be disconnected and the voltmeter would read zero. Shorting either bulb would allow current through the other bulb. The consistent fault is X open: C.

2013|paper-1a|34.question:
U92238 undergoes α–β–β–α decay to become nuclide X. Find the atomic number and mass number of X, in that order.

A. 90; 230

B. 90; 234

C. 88; 230

D. 88; 234

Two α and two β⁻ decays give A = 238−8 = 230 and Z = 92−4+2 = 90. In the requested order Z, A the answer is 90, 230: A.

2013|paper-1a|35.question:
* Polonium-210 is a pure α-emitter with half-life 140 days and decays to stable lead. A sample initially contains 420 mg of pure polonium-210. Estimate the mass of polonium-210 remaining after 70 days.

The remaining isotope mass follows m = m₀ 2−t/T. Thus m = 420×2−70/140 = 420/√2 ≈ 297 mg: B.

Radioactive decay is exponential, not linear. Half of a half-life does not mean half of the usual 50% loss, so 315 mg is incorrect. The question asks for remaining polonium, not total polonium plus lead.

2013|paper-1a|36.question:
* The Sun releases energy by thermonuclear fusion while its mass decreases. Its average power is 3.8×1026 W. Estimate its mass decrease in one second.

A. 4.2×106 kg

B. 4.2×109 kg

C. 1.3×1015 kg

D. 1.3×1018 kg

In 1 s the energy released is E = Pt = 3.8×1026 J. Mass-energy equivalence gives Δm = E/c².

Using c = 3.0×108 m s−1, Δm = (3.8×1026)/(9.0×1016) = 4.22×109 kg: B. Square the entire speed of light, including its power of ten.

2013|paper-1a|4.question:
* Vessel X of volume V and vessel Y of volume 2V are connected by a short narrow tube. Initially tap S is closed; the same ideal gas at the same temperature is contained in X and Y at pressures 2p and p respectively. S is opened and equilibrium is reached at unchanged temperature. Which statement is INCORRECT?

A. Before S is opened, both vessels contain the same number of gas molecules.

B. Before S is opened, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules in both vessels is the same.

C. When S is opened, a net flow of gas from X to Y occurs.

D. At equilibrium the gas pressure becomes (3/2)p.

Initially NXkT = (2p)V and NYkT = p(2V), so the numbers are equal. Equal temperature also means equal average molecular kinetic energy. The initial pressure difference drives a net flow from X to Y.

Conserve total molecules at fixed T: pf(3V) = 2pV + p(2V) = 4pV, giving pf = 4p/3, not 3p/2. The incorrect statement is D; an unweighted mean of pressures is invalid for unequal volumes.

2013|paper-1a|5.question:
A block of weight 20 N is suspended by a light string from the ceiling. A force F displaces the block to one side with the string making 25° with the vertical, as shown. Find F.

2013|paper-1a|6.question:
O is the centre of a regular hexagon. A particle at O is subject to the six forces shown. The resultant force on the particle is

OD and OF are separated by 120°. Their equal 3 N vectors give 2(3)cos 60° = 3 N along the bisector OE. Add the remaining 3 N along OE to obtain 6 N along OE: D.

2013|paper-1a|7.question:
A block on a rough horizontal surface moves left with constant speed under the horizontal forces 2 N and 12 N shown. If the 12 N force is suddenly removed, what is the net force on the block at that instant?

B. 10 N

D. 2 N

2013|paper-1a|8.question:
A particle is released from rest at X. It takes time t1 to fall from X to Y and time t2 from Y to Z. If XY : YZ = 9 : 16, find t1 : t2. Neglect air resistance.

A supermarket trolley rests on the ground. Cylindrical wheels X and Y are 0.7 m apart. Its total loaded weight is 154 N and its centre of gravity G is a horizontal distance 0.5 m from Y. What is the ground reaction on wheel X?

2013|paper-1b|1.question:
A rooftop solar water heater heats 1.5 m3 of water to 80°C during the day. At night, water from the storage tank circulates through radiators to warm the rooms.

Given: density of water = 1000 kg m−3; specific heat capacity = 4200 J kg−1 °C−1.

(a) During transfer of water, 15% of the energy is lost. Find the heat released to the rooms as the water cools to 60°C. (3 marks)

(b) At night the radiators maintain an average output power of 4.5 kW. For how many hours can this continue until the water reaches 60°C? (2 marks)

(c) The actual heat-release rate gradually decreases over this period. Explain why. (1 mark)
2013|paper-1b|1.official:
(a) Q = (1.5×1000)×4200×(80−60)×(1−15%) = 1.07×108 J. [1M+1M+1A; 3 marks]

(b) t = (1.07×108)/(4.5×103)/3600 = 6.61 hours. [1M+1A]

(c) Heat-transfer rate drops as water temperature drops / room temperature rises / temperature difference drops. [1A]
2013|paper-1b|1.reasoning:
(a) Convert volume to mass: m = ρV = 1500 kg. Water loses mcΔθ = 1.26×108 J, but only 85% reaches the rooms. Useful heat is 1.071×108 J.

(b) Use useful heat with the radiator output power: t = Q/P = 23800 s = 6.61 h. Keep the unrounded heat in calculation; do not subtract the 15% loss a second time.

(c) Heat transfer is driven by temperature difference. Cooling water (and warming rooms) reduces that difference, so the instantaneous power falls even though an average power was used in (b).

2013|paper-1b|10.question:

(a)(i) Find R at 25°C. (1 mark)

(a)(ii) Find the potential difference VAB at 25°C. (2 marks)

(b) Kelly measures VAB with a voltmeter of about 1 kΩ resistance. Despite careful measurement, its reading differs slightly from (a). Explain why and suggest how to improve accuracy. (3 marks)

(c)(i) VAB drives an electronic switch connected across AB, turning a fan on when VAB is 6.0 V or above. Use the graph to find the minimum temperature needed to keep the fan on. Show your working. (2 marks)

(c)(ii) Without additional components, complete the new circuit to turn on a heating device when temperature falls below a certain value. Explain the action; no calculation is required. (3 marks)
2013|paper-1b|10.official:
(a)(i) 80 Ω. [1A]

(a)(ii) VAB = 12×120/(80+120) = 7.2 V. [1M+1A]

(b) The voltmeter is parallel to 120 Ω, reducing the equivalent resistance across AB below 120 Ω [1A], so VAB is lower than expected. [1A] Use a voltmeter with much larger resistance, e.g. a 10 MΩ digital meter. [1A]

(c)(i) 12×120/(R+120) = 6.0, so R = 120 Ω. [1A] Corresponding temperature = 16°C. [1A]
